issues.item: Catastrophising Others: I worry obsessively about bad things happening to people I care about
issues.explanation: 'Catastrophising Others' is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile and the trauma type. The other items center on childhood physical abuse, mistrust, touch-sensitivity, fragmented memory, guilt, and self-damage; obsessive worry about harm befalling loved ones points to a different threat theme and is not supported by the appraisals or memory content.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: 'Door and Lock Checking' suggests a home-intrusion/security threat theme. In this profile, threat is otherwise expressed as interpersonal danger cues (unexpected touch, ominous silence) linked to caregiver abuse. Without matching appraisals or memory content about break-ins or external intruders, this item is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
David presents as a meticulously dressed man of 55, his success as a fashion designer evident in the quiet confidence of his bespoke suit. Yet, beneath the curated exterior is a profound and long-standing distress rooted in events from his childhood. For decades, he managed to build a life around the trauma, but now feels his control is slipping. The memories of the physical abuse he endured from his father are not a coherent narrative but a collection of sensory fragments and disjointed scenes. He speaks of it with a strange detachment, as if narrating a film about a different boy, feeling completely numb to the events he describes. He can recall the pattern of the wallpaper in his childhood bedroom with perfect clarity, but not the sequence of what happened on any given night. This emotionless recall is sometimes punctuated by a sudden, overwhelming wave of guilt, a feeling that he must have done something wrong to deserve it, a thought that loops for hours.

The abuse often took place in the dead of night, and the silence preceding it became the most potent signal of danger. His father would move through the house without a sound, and that heavy, listening quiet is something David’s nervous system has never forgotten. Now, even in the safety of his own spacious downtown loft, an unusual silence makes him feel a palpable sense of dread, as if something terrible is about to happen. He keeps music playing constantly, even when he sleeps, to fill the void. He remains on high alert, checking the locks on his door multiple times before bed and feeling a persistent sense of being on guard. He has come to believe that people cannot be trusted, a conviction that contributed significantly to the dissolution of his marriage years ago. He finds himself dwelling on perceived betrayals, replaying arguments with his ex-wife or slights from business partners in his mind, a cycle of blame that offers no relief. Late at night, the blame turns inward, and he is consumed by thoughts of what he did wrong as a child, what he could have done differently to stop what happened.

His work, once a refuge of control and creativity, has become another source of anxiety. The open-plan, collaborative nature of his design studio means people are constantly moving around him. An unexpected touch, even a well-intentioned hand on his shoulder from his assistant, can trigger an explosive startle response. He reacts with an audible gasp and physically recoils, a reaction that feels utterly beyond his control and deeply shameful. He sees the confusion and concern on his colleagues’ faces and is certain that his reactions are proof that he is, in his own words, “going crazy.” He has come to believe that the boy who was hurt all those years ago fundamentally changed him for the worse, that he is permanently damaged goods. To avoid the nightmares that plague him, he has developed a habit of working late into the night, sketching until he is on the verge of collapse, hoping exhaustion will grant him a dreamless sleep.

David sought therapy after a recent incident at his studio. A young intern, eager to show him a new fabric, approached him silently from behind and gently touched his arm to get his attention. David’s reaction was more severe than ever before; he cried out and stumbled backward, knocking over a mannequin. The entire studio fell silent. The intern was mortified, and David was consumed by a humiliation so profound it left him unable to work for the rest of the day. He realised he could no longer contain the chaos within. He came to his first session stating that he is afraid of losing his mind and, with it, the career that is his last remaining source of identity. His greatest fear is that he is irreparable, but he holds a fragile hope that he might one day be able to sit in a quiet room and feel peace instead of terror.
